    AI Overview
    Measles is a highly contagious respiratory viral infection causing high fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a characteristic rash, often leading to serious complications like pneumonia or encephalitis. Caused by the measles virus, it spreads easily via airborne droplets when an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes. Treatment is primarily supportive, focusing on symptom relief, hydration, and Vitamin A supplementation. Vaccination with the MMR vaccine is the best protection. 
    Key Information on Measles 
    • Symptoms: Initial symptoms include a high fever, runny nose, cough, and red, watery eyes. Small white spots (Koplik spots) may appear inside the mouth 2-3 days after symptoms start. A characteristic red, blotchy rash appears 3-5 days after initial symptoms, usually starting on the face and spreading downward.
    • Causes and Transmission: The measles virus causes the infection, which lives in the mucus of the nose and throat. It is highly contagious, often infecting 90% of unvaccinated people close to an infected person. It spreads via coughing or sneezing, and the virus can remain active in the air or on surfaces for up to two hours.
    • Infectious Period: Infected individuals can spread the virus four days before the rash appears and up to four days after.
    • Complications: Measles can be dangerous, leading to severe issues such as ear infections, diarrhea, pneumonia (the most common cause of death), and brain inflammation (encephalitis). It is most severe in infants, children under 5, adults over 20, and pregnant individuals.
    • Treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment for measles. Care focuses on relieving symptoms, which includes rest, hydration, and managing fever. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), Vitamin A supplements are recommended for all children with acute measles.
    • Prevention: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention | CDC (.gov) recommends two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine for children, with the first dose between 12-15 months and the second between 4-6 years. 
    When to Seek Care
    If you or your child has symptoms, contact a doctor immediately. Seek emergency care for difficulty breathing, confusion, or severe dehydration. 
    For further information, you can consult resources from the Mayo Clinic, CDPH (.gov), National Foundation for Infectious Diseases, and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (.gov).

    A story is circulating about vaccinated health care workers in Utah getting measles and going to work, not realizing infection was possible despite being vaccinated. Naturally, it’s raising a lot of questions. First things first, the MMR vaccine works extremely well, but no vaccine is perfect. A vaccinated person is about 35 times less likely to get measles, though a small percentage can still get infected. That doesn’t mean the vaccine failed. Its primary job is to prevent severe illness, hospitalization, and death. We’re also seeing more measles right now than the U.S. has seen in over 30 years. More virus circulating means more exposure, and more exposure means more breakthrough cases. That’s expected. Exposure level matters, too, especially for health care workers facing intense, prolonged contact.
